title: Peer Pressure Between Agents Silently Breaks Conformal Prediction Guarantees
plain: Researchers demonstrate that conformal prediction certificates calibrated for a large language model answering alone lose their validity when the same model observes peer agents unanimously asserting a wrong answer, a mechanism they term score-mechanism shift. angles.claim: Any conformal prediction calibration done on single-agent outputs must be treated as invalid the moment agents can observe peer answers before finalizing.
angles.audience: AI engineering leads in utilities using multi-agent LLM pipelines with escalation controls
angles.rank_reason: Directly changes what must be checked before Monday: recalibrate under peer-visible conditions or stop trusting the guarantee, and the article demonstrates the mechanism and the numeric drop.

angles.claim: Monitoring average coverage as a safety signal is itself a vulnerability, since an attacker can cut coverage on low-confidence items nearly in half while the average looks fine.
angles.audience: Directors who ask what metric proves the escalation control is working
angles.rank_reason: Gives the director a concrete Thursday question about subgroup coverage rather than aggregate coverage, backed directly by the 87% to 47% figure in the source.

angles.claim: An escalation-on-uncertainty design is not a safety backstop if peer pressure can make the model falsely confident enough to skip escalation entirely.
angles.audience: Engineers designing human-review triggers in multi-agent systems
angles.rank_reason: Narrower than the first two since it addresses one downstream consequence of the same finding rather than the calibration assumption itself, but still actionable for anyone relying on escalation logic as a control.
